Long Video Understanding vs. Camera Roll VQA

Two ways of asking a machine to remember what it saw — one continuous stream, one scattered archive.
By Thao Nguyen · draft, June 2026
Work in progress · this post grows in 3 steps

Both long video understanding and camera roll VQA ask a model to answer questions over a large stream of visual content that no longer fits in a single context window. But the two settings differ in almost everything that matters for how we build the data: where the visuals come from, how they are ordered in time, how personal they are, and what kind of question a human would actually want to ask. This post maps out those differences.

We are writing it in three steps:

Step 1 · in this draft
Survey
A curated list of datasets / benchmarks for each domain, with links to project pages, code, and papers.
Step 2 · in this draft
Question / task analysis
Pulled questions from 7 long-video sets and compared their task types against camroll.
Step 3 · later
Core challenges
What fundamentally differs in how people construct these benchmarks — and why.

The two paradigms at a glance

Before the long lists, here is the contrast in one table. (We will revisit and sharpen these claims with data in Steps 2 and 3.)

Dimension Long Video Understanding Camera Roll VQA
Input unit One temporally continuous video (a stream of frames). A set of discrete personal photos, sparsely sampled across life.
Temporal structure Dense & ordered: seconds→minutes→hours within one event/story. Fragmented: thousands of photos over 2–6 years, many disjoint events.
Scale Minutes to ~2 hours of footage per item. Hundreds–thousands of images per user (often 1–10M tokens if naively fed).
Source YouTube, movies/TV, egocentric recordings, surveillance. Real users' phone camera rolls (+ curated public photo streams).
Personalization Low — content & answers are largely shared across examples. High — ~90% of gold answers are unique to a single user.
Typical query MCQ on plot, action, temporal order, fine-grained perception. First-person semantic & episodic questions ("What did I eat after…?").
Core difficulty Long-context reasoning over a continuous stream. Navigate / retrieve over huge personal memory + personalized grounding.

That heterogeneity is itself a clue for Step 3: the personal-memory community hasn't yet agreed on what "one example" even is.

Step 2 · Question / task analysis

To move past hand-waving, we downloaded the question text only (no videos) from seven long-video benchmarks and lined them up against camroll. Crucially, camroll is not one benchmark — it is a suite of five sub-benchmarks (ATM-Bench, DIS-Bench, Persona-MME, In-house, photo-bench), each with its own question style. We treat each as a separate set below. In total that is ~102k questions: Video-MME (2,700), LongVideoBench (6,678), LVBench (1,549), EgoLifeQA (500*), VideoOdyssey (2,680), MovieQA (14,944), EPIC-KITCHENS narrations (67,217), and the five camroll subsets (5,857 combined). We then measured answer format, the question-word mix, and two hallmarks of personal memory: first-person framing and episodic / personal-time references.

The headline. Almost every long-video benchmark is third-person multiple-choice over a single video. Every camroll subset — and the egocentric outlier EgoLifeQA — instead makes the user the subject, and none of them use MCQ. But the camroll subsets are far from uniform: they span semantic self-facts (In-house, 96% first-person), episodic recall (ATM-Bench), conversational persona (Persona-MME), photo retrieval (DIS-Bench), and terse tag-style prompts (photo-bench).

Different labeling axes

The clearest tell is how each community names its question types. Long-video sets label by visual skill (object / action / temporal / OCR). camroll & EgoLifeQA label by memory function (recall, entity log, relationships, habits) — a different axis entirely.

Representative questions, side by side

camroll (ours) · five subsets, one per style

ATM-Bench · episodic recall“Today is May 2, 2024 — I had a formal in Peterhouse last week; what was the name of that red dessert with strawberry I had near the end?”
In-house · semantic self-fact“What is my occupation?”
Persona-MME · conversational“Hey, that picture of the two giraffes I sent over a week ago… remind me, what was the thought I had right when I sent it?”
DIS-Bench · retrieval“Find photos from the musical performance identified by the blue-and-white event logo, where only the lead singer appears on stage.”
photo-bench · tag prompt“girl in purple sweater” · “cluttered desk”

Long-video · third-person MCQ

Video-MME“…which decoration has the largest number?” — (A) Apples (B) Candles (C) Berries (D) Same
MovieQA“Why does Hook leave Eamon’s apartment?” — (1 of 5 options)
EgoLifeQA“Who used the screwdriver first?” — (A–D)
LongVideoBench“In the video, which subtitles appear at the same time as the man with black hair, dressed in grey, on stage?”
Takeaway for Step 3. The split is not just “harder questions” — it is a different question-design philosophy. Long-video benchmarks optimize for clean, gradeable MCQs about a shared video; camera-roll VQA wants open, first-person, time-anchored answers that only the owner could verify. And notice that camroll itself is not one task but five — episodic recall, retrieval, conversational persona, semantic self-facts, and tag prompts. The personal-memory space hasn’t converged on a single format, which is exactly what makes constructing these benchmarks hard — the subject of Step 3.

Method & caveats. Questions pulled from each benchmark's released annotations (HuggingFace / GitHub), text only. * EgoLifeQA is the public JAKE subset (500 of ~3,000 Q). MovieQA counts include train+val+test (test answers are gated). EPIC-KITCHENS is action narration, included as the egocentric “ground-truth events” contrast, not a QA set. First-person / episodic are measured by keyword matching, so treat them as lower bounds.

Zooming in: EgoLifeQA vs. camroll

Of all seven long-video sets, EgoLifeQA is the nearest neighbour to camroll: both are egocentric, first-person, and episodic, and both ask a model to remember things scattered far back in a personal history. They are the only two sets where “I” and “when” dominate. So it is worth asking: are they the same task? Looking at the actual questions, they turn out to be two different flavours of personal memory.

DimensionEgoLifeQAcamroll (ours)
Input shapeContinuous head-mounted video stream (the wearer's POV)Scattered photo archive (a phone camera roll)
Scale & span6 wearers, ~44 h each, one shared week50 users, ~31k photos, 2–6 years each
Subject of the questionThe social scene — what the housemates did (Tasha, Alice, “Me”…)The user's own life — their facts, possessions, trips, thoughts
Answer format4-way MCQ (A–D)Open-ended + retrieval (no options)
Temporal anchorRelative: “before”, “first”, “earlier” + frame timestampsAbsolute: calendar dates & named events (“BMVC 2024”, “May 2”)
Evidence distanceMedian ~1.8 h back; 38% from an earlier daySpans years; cued by the date/event named in the question
Modality needed40% need audio, 64% need person-IDPhotos (+ persona text); no audio
Memory typeFine-grained episodic within one weekEpisodic across years + semantic self-knowledge
EgoLifeQA — how far back the evidence sits (share of questions)
The answer is rarely “on screen now”: ~76% of questions need evidence from over an hour earlier or a previous day — the same long-horizon recall camroll demands across years. (JAKE subset, 464 of 500 Q with timestamps)

Left: questions are about other people in the wearer’s view, answered by picking a name (A–D). Right: questions are about the user themselves, answered in free text. Both look backward in time.
The key difference: social vs. autobiographical memory. EgoLifeQA is largely third-party memory captured from a first-person camera — who did what around the wearer during one intense shared week, often needing audio and face/name recognition. camroll is autobiographical — the user's own facts, possessions and events across years, answered openly and verifiable only by them. Same egocentric, long-horizon spirit; opposite question subject and answer style.

How this map was made · technical details

Corpus. 10,394 questions — EgoLifeQA, the five camroll sub-benchmarks, and two generic long-video benchmarks (Video-MME, LongVideoBench) for contrast. Only question text is embedded. Per source:

  • EgoLifeQA — 500 (participant A1 / JAKE)
  • ATM-Bench — 1,013
  • DIS-Bench — 122
  • Persona-MME — 2,034
  • In-house — 1,500
  • photo-bench — 1,188
  • Video-MME — 2,700 (full test set)
  • LongVideoBench — 1,337 (val split, has answers)

On EgoLifeQA's size. EgoLifeQA is designed as ~3,000 questions (6 participants × ~500). Only participant A1 / JAKE's 500 are publicly released with ground-truth answers; the other ~2,500 are held out as the EgoLife Challenge test set. The questions were AI-generated (GPT-4o, ~100K candidates) then human-curated to 500 by an external annotation team — so for EgoLifeQA the annotator ≠ the camera wearer, which is why its questions read as third-party “who-did-what” rather than autobiographical.

Embedding & projection. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-d, L2-normalized) → UMAP (n_neighbors=25, min_dist=0.12, metric="cosine", random_state=42), coords min–max normalized to [0,1]. Rendered on an HTML5 <canvas> with vanilla JS, data inline.

Read distances loosely: UMAP keeps local neighbourhoods but distorts global gaps; the model is general-purpose, so the layout reflects surface phrasing + topic as much as task type. An exploratory lens, not a metric space.

Same color key as the full map. Three sources only: EgoLifeQA (blue, social MCQ recall), ATM-Bench (orange, episodic “when/where did I”), and In-house (green, self-facts). Watch whether EgoLifeQA forms its own island or threads into ATM-Bench's episodic questions, and where the In-house self-facts sit relative to both.

The two only partly overlap: ~71% of EgoLifeQA and ~74% of camroll sit in neighbourhoods made almost entirely of their own kind. Reading the non-overlapping regions tells you what each world asks that the other simply can't:

🔵 Only in EgoLifeQA — social, multi-person recall

the isolated blue island · mostly RelationMap + EventRecall · 95% need person-ID, 55% need audio
  • Who did what with / for whom: “Who helped Alice take off the bracelet?”
  • Group conversation recall: “After Lucia said she wanted fruit, what fruit did Katrina mention?”
  • Other people's habits & plans: “What kind of music does Lucia like to dance to?”

camroll has no analog: it never tracks other people's interactions or speech.

🟠 Only in camroll — autobiographical travel & self-facts

the isolated orange/green region · 47% name a date, 33% name a place/trip
  • Trips across cities & years: “Where did I have my last meal in Changsha before leaving?”
  • Photo retrieval (no options): “Help me find the photo I took of the White Cliffs of Dover.”
  • Reading text in the world: “What does the sign say marking the Dead Sea's elevation?”
  • Long-range self-knowledge: “What is my likely occupation?”, “What stage of school is my daughter in?”

EgoLifeQA has no analog: one shared week can't hold years of travel, purchases or life-state.

🟣 Where they meet — first-person habits & everyday recall

the mixed band (~122 questions, evenly EgoLifeQA / camroll) · 70% say “I / me / my”, 27% are “when / last time” · on EgoLifeQA's side need-name drops to 36% (from 95%)

When EgoLifeQA drops the social/name dimension and camroll drops the long calendar span, they ask nearly the same thing — questions about the user's own routines, preferences, and recent everyday events:

EgoLifeQA side
  • “What do I usually do after picking up glasses no one is wearing?”
  • “Who do I usually sit with during meals?”
  • “What was the tablet used for last time?”
camroll side
  • “What flavor of food do I prefer?”
  • “Do I often attend my friends' birthday parties?”
  • “What did I do the day after I took that photo?”

This is the genuine common ground both communities care about: habit / preference / routine self-knowledge and recent first-person episodic recall — the “personal assistant” core, minus EgoLifeQA's group-social puzzles and camroll's multi-year travel log.

Step 3 · How people approach EgoLifeQA

Before contrasting how the egocentric-video and camera-roll communities build systems, we surveyed everything that builds on or cites EgoLife. Most citations are benchmarks or unrelated egocentric topics; below are the 22 that propose an approach to long-horizon egocentric / personal-memory QA. 5 report numbers directly on EgoLifeQA (green chip); the rest target sibling benchmarks. The dominant recipe is an agentic memory + tool-calling loop: a planner/LLM that decomposes a question and invokes named perception / retrieval tools (RAG, video-LLM, VLM, visual / audio / entity-graph search…) over a structured memory.

What the survey shows.

  • The EgoLifeQA leaderboard is agentic. Every system that beats EgoButler on EgoLifeQA — Ego-R1, EGAgent, WorldMM, MAGIC-Video — wraps a frozen (or RL-tuned) backbone in a plan → call-tool → analyze → answer loop. The tools are remarkably consistent: a text/RAG retriever, a video-LLM / VLM for visual detail, and increasingly an entity-graph search for "who / what / when" relational queries.
  • Memory is converging on graphs and hierarchies. Entity scene graphs (EGAgent), multimodal memory graphs (MAGIC-Video, M3-Agent), and three-store episodic/semantic/visual designs (WorldMM) dominate; hierarchical multi-scale memory (VAM, VideoLucy, Ego-R1's H-RAG) is the other pole.
  • Training, when present, is RL on small sets. Ego-R1 (SFT→RL), TaskMem (RL memorization policy), M3-Agent (RL), EgoVITA (GRPO), Time-R1 (verifiable-reward RL) — all on 2.5k–47k curated or self-generated samples, not web-scale data.

Tools / memory / training for the six core EgoLifeQA systems (EgoButler, Ego-R1, EGAgent, MAGIC-Video, WorldMM, VAM, VideoLucy, M3-Agent) are taken from the full papers; the rest are from abstracts, with "needs full read" flagging any column the abstract didn't pin down.
